claim: Cognitive control resolves conflicts between task-relevant and task-irrelevant information to enable goal-directed behavior.
source: Cognitive control resolves conflicts between task-relevant and -irrelevant information to enable goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that defines the concept of cognitive control.

claim: Conflicts can arise from different sources such as sensory input and internal representations.
source: As conflicts can arise from different sources (e.g., sensory input, internal representations), how a limited set of cognitive control processes can effectively address diverse conflicts remains a major challenge.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the nature of conflicts.

claim: Different conflicts can be parameterized and represented as distinct points in a low-dimensional cognitive space according to the cognitive space theory.
source: Based on the cognitive space theory, different conflicts can be parameterized and represented as distinct points in a (low-dimensional) cognitive space, which can then be resolved by a limited set of cognitive control processes working along the dimensions.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the cognitive space theory framework.

claim: Conflicts similar in their sources are represented similarly in the cognitive space.
source: It leads to a hypothesis that conflicts similar in their sources are also represented similarly in the cognitive space.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis derived from the cognitive space theory.

claim: Human performance supports that different types of conflicts are organized based on their similarity.
source: Both human performance and fMRI activity patterns in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex support that different types of conflicts are organized based on their similarity, thus suggesting cognitive space as a principle for representing conflicts.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on behavioral data analysis.

claim: fMRI activity patterns in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex support that different types of conflicts are organized based on their similarity.
source: Both human performance and fMRI activity patterns in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex support that different types of conflicts are organized based on their similarity, thus suggesting cognitive space as a principle for representing conflicts.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Task-relevant and task-irrelevant information can come from different sources.
source: As task-relevant and task-irrelevant information can come from different sources, the sources of conflicts and how they should be resolved can vary greatly (Kornblum et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kornblum et al., 1990.

claim: Conflict may occur between items of sensory information, such as between a red light and a police officer signaling cars to pass.
source: For example, the conflict may occur between items of sensory information, such as between a red light and a police officer signaling cars to pass.
evidence: This is an illustrative example provided in the text.

claim: Conflict may occur between sensory and motor information, such as when a voice on the left asks you to turn right.
source: Alternatively, conflict may occur between sensory and motor information, such as when a voice on the left asks you to turn right.
evidence: This is an illustrative example provided in the text.

claim: Domains of conflicts include experimental paradigm, sensory modality, and conflict type regarding dimensional overlap of conflict processes.
source: Examples of the domains of conflicts include experimental paradigm (Freitas et al., 2007; Magen and Cohen, 2007), sensory modality (Hazeltine et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2017), or conflict type regarding the dimensional overlap of conflict processes (Jiang and Egner, 2014; Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Domain-general cognitive control theories posit that the frontoparietal cortex adaptively encodes task information and can flexibly implement control strategies for different types of conflicts.
source: On the one hand, the domain-general cognitive control theories posit that the frontoparietal cortex adaptively encodes task information and can thus flexibly implement control strategies for different types of conflicts.
evidence: This is a description of domain-general theories based on established literature.

claim: Generalizable control adjustment across different conflict types supports domain-general cognitive control theories.
source: This is supported by the generalizable control adjustment (i.e., encountering a conflict trial from one type can facilitate conflict resolution of another type) (Freitas et al., 2007; Kan et al., 2013) and similar neural patterns (Peterson et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2020) across distinct conflict tasks.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Similar neural patterns across distinct conflict tasks support domain-general cognitive control theories.
source: This is supported by the generalizable control adjustment (i.e., encountering a conflict trial from one type can facilitate conflict resolution of another type) (Freitas et al., 2007; Kan et al., 2013) and similar neural patterns (Peterson et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2020) across distinct conflict tasks.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Frontoparietal brain regions/networks are widely involved in multiple control demands beyond the conflict domain.
source: A broader domain-general view holds that the frontoparietal brain regions/networks are widely involved in multiple control demands well beyond the conflict domain (Assem et al., 2020; Cole et al., 2013), which explains the remarkable flexibility in human behaviors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When handling multiple task demands simultaneously, the efficiency of both tasks would be impaired due to resource competition or interference in domain-general processes.
source: However, since domain-general processes are by definition likely shared by different tasks, when we need to handle multiple task demands at the same time, the efficiency of both tasks would be impaired due to resource competition or interference (Musslick and Cohen, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Musslick and Cohen, 2021.

claim: Domain-general processes are evolutionarily less advantageous for humans to deal with diverse situations requiring high efficiency.
source: Therefore, the domain-general processes are evolutionarily less advantageous for humans to deal with the diverse situations requiring high efficiency (Cosmides and Tooby, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cosmides and Tooby, 1994.

claim: Domain-specific theories argue that different types of conflicts are handled by distinct cognitive control processes.
source: On the other hand, the domain-specific theories argue that different types of conflicts are handled by distinct cognitive control processes (e.g., where and how information processing should be modulated) (Egner, 2008; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of domain-specific theories supported by citations.

claim: According to the domain-specific view, diverse conflict situations require a multitude of preexisting control processes, which is biologically implausible.
source: However, according to the domain-specific view, the diverse conflict situations require a multitude of preexisting control processes, which is biologically implausible (Abrahamse et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Abrahamse et al., 2016.

claim: Cognitive control might be a mixture of domain-general and domain-specific processes.
source: To reconcile the two theories, researchers recently proposed that cognitive control might be a mixture of domain-general and domain-specific processes.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on recent research.

claim: Trial-by-trial adjustment of control can generalize across two conflict domains to different degrees.
source: For instance, Freitas and Clark, 2015 found that trial-by-trial adjustment of control can generalize across two conflict domains to different degrees, leading to domain-general (strong generalization) or domain-specific (weak or no generalization) conclusions depending on the task settings of the consecutive conflicts.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Freitas and Clark, 2015.

claim: Different brain networks may show domain-generality or domain-specificity.
source: Similarly, different brain networks may show domain-generality (i.e., representing multiple conflicts) or domain-specificity (i.e., representing individual conflicts separately) (Jiang and Egner, 2014; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural population activity in the medial frontal cortex can be factorized into orthogonal dimensions encoding both domain-general and domain-specific conflict information.
source: Even within the same brain area (e.g., medial frontal cortex), Fu et al., 2022 found that the neural population activity can be factorized into orthogonal dimensions encoding both domain-general and domain-specific conflict information, which can be selectively read out by downstream brain regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2022.

claim: The cognitive space extends the idea of cognitive map to the representation of abstract information.
source: A construct with a similar function is the cognitive space (Bellmund et al., 2018), which extends the idea of cognitive map (Behrens et al., 2018) to the representation of abstract information.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bellmund et al., 2018 and Behrens et al., 2018.

claim: The representations of different abstract information are organized continuously in the cognitive space.
source: Critically, the cognitive space view holds that the representations of different abstract information are organized continuously and the representational geometry in the cognitive space is determined by the similarity among the represented information (Bellmund et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bellmund et al., 2018.

claim: The representational geometry in the cognitive space is determined by the similarity among the represented information.
source: Critically, the cognitive space view holds that the representations of different abstract information are organized continuously and the representational geometry in the cognitive space is determined by the similarity among the represented information (Bellmund et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bellmund et al., 2018.

claim: Abstract and social information can be represented in a cognitive space in the human brain.
source: In the human brain, it has been shown that abstract (Behrens et al., 2018; Schuck et al., 2016) and social (Park et al., 2020) information can be represented in a cognitive space.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Social hierarchies with two independent scores can be represented in a 2D cognitive space.
source: For example, social hierarchies with two independent scores (e.g., popularity and competence) can be represented in a 2D cognitive space (one dimension for each score), such that each social item can be located by its score in the two dimensions (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2020.

claim: Recent studies have begun to conceptualize different control states within a cognitive space.
source: In the field of cognitive control, recent studies have begun to conceptualize different control states within a cognitive space (Badre et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Badre et al., 2021.

claim: It is possible to manipulate continuous conflict similarity by using a mixture of two independent conflict types with varying ratios.
source: Our recent work (Yang et al., 2021) showed that it is possible to manipulate continuous conflict similarity by using a mixture of two independent conflict types with varying ratios, which can be used to further examine the behavioral and neural evidence for the cognitive space view.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: Abstract task structure could be encoded and implemented by the frontoparietal network.
source: Recent research has suggested that the abstract task structure could be encoded and implemented by the frontoparietal network (Vaidya and Badre, 2022; Vaidya et al., 2021), but whether a similar neural system encodes the cognitive space of cognitive control remains untested.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Vaidya and Badre, 2022 and Vaidya et al., 2021.

claim: Different types of conflicts are represented as points in a cognitive space.
source: Specifically, we hypothesize that different types of conflicts are represented as points in a cognitive space.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis of the study.

claim: The distance between points in the cognitive space scales with the difference in the sources of the conflicts being represented.
source: Importantly, the distance between the points, which reflects the geometry of the cognitive space, scales with the difference in the sources of the conflicts being represented by the points.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesis of the study.

claim: The cognitive space representing different types of conflicts may be located in the frontoparietal network.
source: We further hypothesize that the cognitive space representing different types of conflicts may be located in the frontoparietal network due to its essential roles in conflict resolution (Freund et al., 2021a; Fu et al., 2022) and abstract task representation (Vaidya and Badre, 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The vertical location of the arrow can be incongruent with the direction, resulting in spatial Stroop conflict.
source: On one hand, the vertical location of the arrow can be incongruent with the direction (e.g., an up-pointing arrow on the lower half of the screen), resulting spatial Stroop conflict (Liu et al., 2004; Lu and Proctor, 1995).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by citations.

claim: The horizontal location of the arrow can be incongruent with the response key, causing Simon conflict.
source: On the other hand, the horizontal location of the arrow can be incongruent with the response key (e.g., an arrow requiring left response presented on the right side of the screen), thus causing Simon conflict (Lu and Proctor, 1995; Simon and Small, 1969).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by citations.

claim: As the arrow location rotates from the horizontal axis to the vertical axis, spatial Stroop conflict increases and Simon conflict decreases.
source: As the arrow location rotates from the horizontal axis to the vertical axis, spatial Stroop conflict increases, and Simon conflict decreases.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: The 10 possible locations of the arrow give rise to five conflict types with unique blend of spatial Stroop and Simon conflicts.
source: Therefore, the 10 possible locations of the arrow give rise to five conflict types with unique blend of spatial Stroop and Simon conflicts (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by a citation.

claim: A 1D cognitive space can represent all five conflict types.
source: As the increase in spatial Stroop conflict is highly correlated with the decrease in Simon conflict, we can use a 1D cognitive space to represent all five conflict types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Participants responded more slowly in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types in experiment 1.
source: Simple effect analyses showed that participants responded more slowly in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types, pFDRs<0.001.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 1.

claim: The congruency effects of StHSmL, StMSmM, and StLSmH were significantly larger than that of spatial Stroop in RT in experiment 1.
source: Additionally, the congruency effects the StHSmL, StMSmM, and StLSmH were significantly larger than that of spatial Stroop, and the congruency effects of StHSmL and StMSmM were significantly larger than that of Simon, pFDRs<0.05.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 1.

claim: Participants were more error-prone in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types in experiment 1.
source: Simple effect analyses showed that participants were more error-prone in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types, pFDRs<0.001.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 1.

claim: The congruency effects of StHSmL, StMSmM, and StLSmH were significantly larger than that of spatial Stroop in ER in experiment 1.
source: The congruency effects of StHSmL, StMSmM, and StLSmH were significantly larger than that of spatial Stroop, and the congruency effects of StMSmM and StLSmH were significantly larger than that of Simon, pFDRs<0.05.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 1.

claim: Participants responded more slowly in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types in experiment 2.
source: Simple effect analyses showed that participants responded more slowly in incongruent conditions than in congruent conditions for all conflict types, pFDRs<0.001.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 2.

claim: All conflict types showed a larger ER in incongruent than congruent conditions in experiment 2, except type 1 which showed marginal significance.
source: All the types showed a larger ER in incongruent than congruent conditions (pFDRs<0.001), except that type 1 only showed a marginal significance (pFDR=0.062).
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 2.

claim: The CSE diminishes if two consecutive trials have different conflict types.
source: It has been shown that the CSE diminishes if the two consecutive trials have different conflict types (Akçay and Hazeltine, 2011; Egner et al., 2007; Torres-Quesada et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The CSE measured in both RT and ER scaled with conflict similarity in experiment 1.
source: As shown in Figure 2, the CSE, measured in both RT and ER, scaled with conflict similarity.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral data analysis in experiment 1, supported by Figure 2.

claim: Conflict similarity significantly modulated the CSE in RT in experiment 1.
source: The results showed a significant effect of conflict similarity [RT: β = 0.10 ± 0.01, t(1719.7) = 15.82, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.120; ER: β = 0.15 ± 0.02, t(204.5) = 7.84, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.085, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B/E].
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effect model analysis in experiment 1.

claim: Conflict similarity significantly modulated the CSE in ER in experiment 1.
source: The results showed a significant effect of conflict similarity [RT: β = 0.10 ± 0.01, t(1719.7) = 15.82, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.120; ER: β = 0.15 ± 0.02, t(204.5) = 7.84, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.085, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B/E].
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effect model analysis in experiment 1.

claim: The conflict similarity modulation effect remained significant after regressing out the influence of physical proximity between stimuli in experiment 1.
source: The conflict similarity modulation effect remained significant after regressing out the influence of physical proximity between the stimuli of consecutive trials [RT: β = 0.09 ± 0.01, t(1902.4) = 13.74, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.025; ER: β = 0.09 ± 0.01, t(249.3) = 7.66, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.018].
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis in experiment 1.

claim: The two-stage analysis showed a strong effect of conflict similarity in RT in experiment 1.
source: The two-stage analysis also showed a strong effect of conflict similarity [RT: β = 0.58 ± 0.04, t(67.5) = 14.74, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.388; ER: β = 0.36 ± 0.05, t(40.3) = 7.01, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.320, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A/D].
evidence: This is a result from the two-stage analysis in experiment 1.

claim: Individual modulation effects of conflict similarity were positively correlated between the two approaches in experiment 1.
source: Importantly, individual modulation effects of conflict similarity were positively correlated between the two approaches (RT: r = 0.48; ER: r = 0.86, both ps<0.003, one-tailed), indicating the consistency of the estimated conflict similarity effects across the two approaches.
evidence: This is a result from comparing two analysis approaches in experiment 1.

claim: The predicted CSE results from leave-one-out analysis were highly correlated with the original data in experiment 1.
source: The predicted results were highly correlated with the original data, with r = 0.87 for the RT and r = 0.84 for the ER, ps<0.001.
evidence: This is a result from the leave-one-out prediction analysis in experiment 1.

claim: The conflict similarity modulation effect does not change across sessions in experiment 1.
source: Results showed no interaction effect in either RT, F(2,76.4) = 1.025, p=0.364, or ER, F(2,49.4) = 0.789, p=0.460. This result suggests that the modulation effect does not change across time.
evidence: This is a result from testing the effect of training across sessions in experiment 1.

claim: Conflict similarity significantly modulated the behavioral CSE in RT in experiment 2.
source: Results showed a significant effect of conflict similarity modulation (RT: β = 0.24 ± 0.04, t(71.7) = 6.36, p<0.001, ηp2 = .096; ER: β = 0.33 ± 0.06, t(175.4) = 5.81, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.124, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C/F), thus replicating the results of experimental 1 and setting the stage for fMRI analysis.
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effect model analysis in experiment 2.

claim: Conflict similarity significantly modulated the behavioral CSE in ER in experiment 2.
source: Results showed a significant effect of conflict similarity modulation (RT: β = 0.24 ± 0.04, t(71.7) = 6.36, p<0.001, ηp2 = .096; ER: β = 0.33 ± 0.06, t(175.4) = 5.81, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.124, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C/F), thus replicating the results of experimental 1 and setting the stage for fMRI analysis.
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effect model analysis in experiment 2.

claim: The conflict similarity modulation effect remained significant after regressing out the influence of physical proximity between stimuli in experiment 2.
source: As in experiment 1, the conflict similarity modulation effect remained significant after regressing out the influence of physical proximity between the stimuli of consecutive trials (RT: β = 0.21 ± 0.02, t(61.0) = 4.71, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.056; ER: β = 0.20 ± 0.03, t(65.0) = 4.16, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.236).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis in experiment 2.

claim: The congruency effect was observed in the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA).
source: Consistent with the literature (Botvinick et al., 2004; Fu et al., 2022), this effect was observed in the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the univariate fMRI analysis, supported by Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The right inferior parietal sulcus (IPS) displayed positive correlation between fMRI activation and Simon conflict.
source: Accordingly, we found the right inferior parietal sulcus (IPS) and the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) displayed positive correlation between fMRI activation and the Simon conflict (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the univariate fMRI analysis, supported by Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) displayed positive correlation between fMRI activation and Simon conflict.
source: Accordingly, we found the right inferior parietal sulcus (IPS) and the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) displayed positive correlation between fMRI activation and the Simon conflict (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the univariate fMRI analysis, supported by Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: No regions showed significant correlation with the spatial Stroop conflict in univariate analysis.
source: We did not observe regions showing significant correlation with the spatial Stroop conflict.
evidence: This is a result from the univariate fMRI analysis.

claim: Neither the right IPS nor the right dmPFC were positively correlated with the behavioral conflict similarity modulation effect.
source: However, none of the two regions (i.e., right IPS and right dmPFC, Figure 3) were positively correlated with the behavioral performance, both uncorrected ps>0.28, one-tailed.
evidence: This is a result from the brain-behavioral correlation analysis.

claim: Representational similarity of BOLD signal patterns significantly covaried with whether two response/spatial location/arrow directions were the same in bilateral motor/visual/somatosensory areas.
source: To validate this method, we applied this analysis to test the effects of response/stimulus features and found that representational similarity of the BOLD signal patterns significantly covaried with whether two response/spatial location/arrow directions were the same most strongly in bilateral motor/visual/somatosensory areas, respectively (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from the validation of the cross-subject RSA method, supported by Figure 5.

claim: In the incongruent condition, the target representation was enhanced in left V4.
source: Results showed that in the incongruent condition, when we employ more cognitive control, the target representation was enhanced [t(72.2) = 2.28, p=0.039, Bonferroni corrected] and both spatial Stroop [t(85.4) = –3.94, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected] and Simon [t(38.9) = –2.80, p=0.012, Bonferroni corrected] distractor representations were suppressed (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis of cross-subject RSA, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: In the incongruent condition, both spatial Stroop and Simon distractor representations were suppressed in left V4.
source: Results showed that in the incongruent condition, when we employ more cognitive control, the target representation was enhanced [t(72.2) = 2.28, p=0.039, Bonferroni corrected] and both spatial Stroop [t(85.4) = –3.94, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected] and Simon [t(38.9) = –2.80, p=0.012, Bonferroni corrected] distractor representations were suppressed (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis of cross-subject RSA, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: Several cortical regions exhibited a statistically significant positive conflict similarity effect on the RSM.
source: The first criterion revealed several cortical regions encoding the conflict similarity, including the frontal eye field (FEF), region 1, Brodmann 8C area (a subregion of dlPFC) (Glasser et al., 2016), a47r, posterior inferior frontal junction (IFJp), anterior intraparietal area (AIP), temporoparietooccipital junction 3 (TPOJ3), PGi, and V3CD in the right hemisphere, and the superior frontal language (SFL) area, 23c, 24dd, 7Am, p32pr, 6r, FOP1, PF, ventromedial visual area (VMV1/2) areas, area 25, MBelt in the left hemisphere (Bonferroni corrected ps<0.05, one-tailed, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate RSA analysis, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: The left SFL, left VMV1, area left 25 and right 8C showed stronger conflict similarity effect in incongruent than congruent conditions.
source: Results revealed that the left SFL, left VMV1, area left 25 and right 8C met this criterion, FDR-corrected ps<0.05, one-tailed, suggesting that the representation of conflict type was strengthened when the conflict was present (e.g., Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate RSA analysis, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: The strength of conflict similarity effect on RSM scaled with the modulation of conflict similarity on the CSE in right 8C.
source: The inter-subject brain–behavioral correlation analysis (criterion 3) showed that the strength of conflict similarity effect on RSM scaled with the modulation of conflict similarity on the CSE (slope in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) in right 8C (r = 0.52, FDR-corrected p=0.015, one-tailed, Figure 6C) only.
evidence: This is a result from the brain-behavioral correlation analysis, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The right 8C but not the left 8C represented the conflict-type similarity.
source: We observed the right 8C but not the left 8C represented the conflict-type similarity.
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate RSA analysis.

claim: None of the left dlPFC regions tested showed representation of conflict type.
source: We tested several regions of the left dlPFC, including the i6-8, 8Av, 8C, p9-46v, 46, 9-46d, and a9-46v (Freund et al., 2021a). We found that none of these regions show the representation of conflict type, all uncorrected ps>0.35.
evidence: This is a result from testing lateralization in the multivariate RSA analysis.

claim: The conflict type is specifically represented in the right dlPFC.
source: These results indicate that the conflict type is specifically represented in the right dlPFC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lateralization analysis.

claim: The right 8C showed a significant conflict similarity effect when using smoothed data.
source: In addition, we repeated the analysis by using data smoothed with a 6 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel. Results showed a significant conflict similarity effect in right 8C, t(1902599.9) = 5.55, p<0.0001, replicating the results on unsmoothed data [t(86.8) = 5.41, p<0.0001].
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis using smoothed data.

claim: The cognitive-space model showed a lower BIC than the Domain-General or Domain-Specific models for the right 8C.
source: Model comparison showed a lower Bayesian information criterion (BIC) in the cognitive-space model (BIC = 5,377,093) than the Domain-General (BIC = 5,377,126) or Domain-Specific (BIC = 5,377,127) models.
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The dimensionality of the representation in the right 8C was 1.19.
source: Further analysis showed the dimensionality of the representation in the right 8C was 1.19, suggesting the cognitive space was close to 1D.
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality analysis.

claim: The cognitive-space model showed better fit than domain-general and domain-specific models when using only incongruent trials.
source: We found a poorer fitting in domain-general (BIC = 1,344,127) and domain-specific (BIC = 1,344,129) models than the cognitive-space model (BIC = 1,344,104).
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis using only incongruent trials.

claim: The right 8C encodes an integrated cognitive space for resolving Stroop and Simon conflicts.
source: These results indicate that the right 8C encodes an integrated cognitive space for resolving Stroop and Simon conflicts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: Increasing fMRI representational similarity between trials with more similar orientations of stimulus location was observed in the occipital cortex.
source: We observed increasing fMRI representational similarity between trials with more similar orientations of stimulus location in the occipital cortex, such as right V1, right V2, right V3, bilateral POS1, and right lateral occipital 2 (LO2) areas (Bonferroni corrected ps<0.05).
evidence: This is a result from the RSA analysis of orientation effects.

claim: The right V1, right V2, right POS1, left IP2, left FEF, and right PF encoded stronger orientation effect in the incongruent than the congruent condition.
source: Results showed that the right V1, right V2, right POS1, left IP2, left FEF, and right PF encoded stronger orientation effect in the incongruent than the congruent condition, FDR-corrected ps<0.05, one-tailed (Table 2, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from the RSA analysis of orientation effects, supported by Figure 7B and Table 2.

claim: None of the orientation-encoding regions positively correlated with the behavioral conflict similarity modulation effect.
source: We then tested whether any of these regions were related to the behavioral performance, and results showed that none of them positively correlated with the behavioral conflict similarity modulation effect, all uncorrected ps>0.18, one-tailed.
evidence: This is a result from the brain-behavioral correlation analysis.

claim: The right V1 and right V2 showed significant representational connectivity with the right 8C.
source: We conducted representational connectivity (i.e., the similarity between two within-subject RSMs of two regions) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) analyses and found that among the orientation effect regions, the right V1 and right V2 showed significant representational connectivity with the right 8C compared to the controlled regions (including those encoding orientation effect but not showing larger encoding strength in incongruent than congruent conditions, as well as eight other regions encoding none of our defined effects in the main RSA, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a result from the representational connectivity analysis.

claim: The right V1 showed higher connectivity with right 8C than the largest connectivity strength in controlled regions.
source: Compared with the largest connectivity strength in the controlled regions (i.e., the left 6ma, β = 0.7991 ± 0.0299), we found higher connectivity in the right V1, β = 0.8633 ± 0.0325, and right V2, β = 0.8772 ± 0.0335 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a result from the representational connectivity analysis, supported by Figure 8.

claim: No univariate congruency effect was observed in the right 8C region.
source: We first tested the univariate congruency effect (incongruent minus congruent) using the parametric modulating GLM1 that was used to estimate fMRI activation levels of conflict type × congruency conditions. We observed no univariate congruency effect in the right 8C region, t(34) = −0.03, p=0.513, one-tailed.
evidence: This is a result from testing whether the multivariate representations differ from congruency effect.

claim: No multivariate congruency effect was observed in the right 8C or any other regions.
source: Neither did we observe a multivariate congruency effect (i.e., the pattern difference between incongruent and congruent conditions compared to that within each condition) in the right 8C or any other regions.
evidence: This is a result from testing whether the multivariate representations differ from congruency effect.

claim: The contrast of incongruent minus congruent on encoding strength of conflict similarity was not correlated with the behavioral congruency effect.
source: We further tested the possibility that the congruency effect may be manifested in behavioral relevance. To this end, we extracted the contrast of incongruent minus congruent on encoding strength of conflict similarity for each subject from the mixed-effect model based on the cross-subject RSA (see 'Representational similarity analysis') and correlated it with the behavioral congruency effect, averaged across the five conflict types (i.e., the main effect reported in Figure 2—figure supplement 1). No significant correlation was observed (r = 0.14, p=0.380, one-tailed).
evidence: This is a result from testing whether the multivariate representations differ from congruency effect.

claim: The neural encoding strength of conflict type does not reflect the level of cognitive control engagement, but the dynamic adjustment of cognitive control instead.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that the neural encoding strength of conflict type does not reflect the level of cognitive control engagement, but the dynamic adjustment of cognitive control instead.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of congruency effects.

claim: No univoxel congruency effect was observed in any of the regions with stronger encoding of orientation in incongruent than congruent condition.
source: Similarly, we tested whether those regions with stronger encoding of orientation in incongruent than congruent condition (i.e., right V1, V2, PF, POS1, and left FEF and IP2) reflect the congruency effect. We observed no univoxel congruency effect in any of these regions, all uncorrected ps>0.89, one-tailed.
evidence: This is a result from testing whether orientation-encoding regions reflect congruency effect.

claim: The orientation effect was not correlated to the behavioral congruency in any of the orientation-encoding regions.
source: In addition, the orientation effect was not correlated to the behavioral congruency in any of the regions, all uncorrected ps>0.074, one-tailed.
evidence: This is a result from testing whether orientation-encoding regions reflect congruency effect.

claim: The encoding of orientation effect did not reflect the encoding of congruency or conflict type.
source: Together with our finding that there was no correlation between the strength of orientation encoding and the conflict similarity modulation on behavioral CSEs in any of these regions (see 'Multivariate patterns of visual and oculomotor areas encode stimulus orientation'), these results indicate that the encoding of orientation effect did not reflect the encoding of congruency or conflict type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of orientation effects.

claim: The encoding of orientations provides perceptual information to determine the conflict type.
source: Instead, we speculate that the encoding of orientations provides perceptual information to determine the conflict type.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the analysis results.

claim: The CSEs were linearly modulated by conflict similarity between consecutive trials.
source: Behaviorally, we found that the CSEs were linearly modulated by conflict similarity between consecutive trials, replicating and extending our previous study (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: BOLD activity patterns in the right dlPFC showed that the representational similarity between conflict types was modulated by their conflict similarity.
source: BOLD activity patterns in the right dlPFC further showed that the representational similarity between conflict types was modulated by their conflict similarity, and that strength of the modulation was positively associated with the modulation of conflict similarity on the behavioral CSE.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings.

claim: The strength of the modulation of representational similarity by conflict similarity was positively associated with the modulation of conflict similarity on the behavioral CSE.
source: BOLD activity patterns in the right dlPFC further showed that the representational similarity between conflict types was modulated by their conflict similarity, and that strength of the modulation was positively associated with the modulation of conflict similarity on the behavioral CSE.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings.

claim: Activity in two brain regions (right IPS and right dlPFC) was parametrically modulated by the conflict type difference.
source: We also observed that activity in two brain regions (right IPS and right dlPFC) was parametrically modulated by the conflict type difference, though they did not directly explain the behavioral results.
evidence: This is a summary of the univariate fMRI findings.

claim: Visual regions encoded the spatial orientation of the stimulus location.
source: Additionally, we found that the visual regions encoded the spatial orientation of the stimulus location, which might provide the essential concrete information to determine the conflict type.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings on orientation encoding.

claim: Conflicts may be organized in a cognitive space that enables a limited set of cognitive control processes to resolve a wide variety of distinct types of conflicts.
source: Together, these results suggest that conflicts may be organized in a cognitive space that enables a limited set of cognitive control processes to resolve a wide variety of distinct types of conflicts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all findings.

claim: The domain-general view of control suggests a common representation for different types of conflicts.
source: Conventionally, the domain-general view of control suggests a common representation for different types of conflicts (Figure 9, left), while the domain-specific view suggests dissociated representations for different types (Figure 9, right).
evidence: This is a description of conventional views, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The domain-specific view suggests dissociated representations for different types of conflicts.
source: Conventionally, the domain-general view of control suggests a common representation for different types of conflicts (Figure 9, left), while the domain-specific view suggests dissociated representations for different types (Figure 9, right).
evidence: This is a description of conventional views, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The CSE systematically varies with conflict similarity level.
source: Here, we parametrically manipulated the similarity of conflict types and found the CSE systematically vary with conflict similarity level, demonstrating that cognitive control is neither purely domain-general nor purely domain-specific, but can be reconciled as a cognitive space (Bellmund et al., 2018; Figure 9, middle).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by Figure 9.

claim: Cognitive control is neither purely domain-general nor purely domain-specific, but can be reconciled as a cognitive space.
source: Here, we parametrically manipulated the similarity of conflict types and found the CSE systematically vary with conflict similarity level, demonstrating that cognitive control is neither purely domain-general nor purely domain-specific, but can be reconciled as a cognitive space (Bellmund et al., 2018; Figure 9, middle).
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the study.

claim: The cognitive-space model explained the representation in right DLPFC better than the domain-general or domain-specific models.
source: The model comparison analysis also showed that the cognitive-space model explained the representation in right DLPFC better than the domain-general or domain-specific models.
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The cognitive space provides a solution to use a single cognitive space organization to encode different types of conflicts that are close or distant to each other.
source: Specifically, the cognitive space provides a solution to use a single cognitive space organization to encode different types of conflicts that are close (domain-general) or distant (domain-specific) to each other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cognitive space framework.

claim: The cognitive space shows the potential for how various conflict types can be coded using limited resources.
source: It also shows the potential for how various conflict types can be coded using limited resources (i.e., as different points in a low-dimensional cognitive space), as suggested by its out-of-sample predictability.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the out-of-sample prediction results.

claim: Geometry can emerge in the cognitive space, which allows for decomposition of a conflict type.
source: Moreover, geometry can also emerge in the cognitive space (Fu et al., 2022), which will allow for decomposition of a conflict type (e.g., how much conflict in each of the dimensions in the cognitive space) so that it can be mapped into the limited set of cognitive control processes.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Fu et al., 2022.

claim: Geometry in the cognitive space enables fast learning of cognitive control settings from similar conflict types by providing a measure of similarity.
source: Such geometry enables fast learning of cognitive control settings from similar conflict types by providing a measure of similarity (e.g., as distance in space).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the cognitive space framework.

claim: The dimensionality of the cognitive space of conflict should not exceed the number of represented features.
source: For example, the Simon conflict can be represented in a space consisting of spatial location, stimulus information, and responses. Thus, the dimensionality of the cognitive space of conflicts should not exceed the number of represented features.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about dimensionality.

claim: Humans selectively represent a small number of features when learning task representations.
source: The dimensionality can be further reduced as humans selectively represent a small number of features when learning task representations (e.g., spatial information is reduced to the horizontal dimension from the 3D space we live in) (Niv, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Niv, 2019.

claim: A low dimensional (1.19D) space was observed representing the five conflict types.
source: Consistently, we observed a low dimensional (1.19D) space representing the five conflict types.
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality analysis.

claim: The reduced dimensionality requires less effort to represent the conflict.
source: The reduced dimensionality does not only require less effort to represent the conflict, but also facilitates generalization of cognitive control settings among different conflict types (Badre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Badre et al., 2021.

claim: The reduced dimensionality facilitates generalization of cognitive control settings among different conflict types.
source: The reduced dimensionality does not only require less effort to represent the conflict, but also facilitates generalization of cognitive control settings among different conflict types (Badre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Badre et al., 2021.

claim: The prefrontal cortex has long been believed to be a key region of cognitive control representation.
source: The prefrontal cortex has long been believed to be a key region of cognitive control representation (Mansouri et al., 2007; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Milner, 1963) and is widely engaged in multiple task demands (Cole et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The prefrontal cortex is widely engaged in multiple task demands.
source: The prefrontal cortex has long been believed to be a key region of cognitive control representation (Mansouri et al., 2007; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Milner, 1963) and is widely engaged in multiple task demands (Cole et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Frontal regions represented latent states that are organized hierarchically.
source: For instance, Vaidya et al., 2021 reported that frontal regions represented latent states that are organized hierarchically.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vaidya et al., 2021.

claim: dlPFC encoded the target and congruency in a typical color-word Stroop task.
source: Freund et al., 2021a showed that dlPFC encoded the target and congruency in a typical color-word Stroop task.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Freund et al., 2021a.

claim: The right dlPFC might flexibly encode a variety of cognitive spaces to meet the dynamic task demands.
source: Taken together, we suggest that the right dlPFC might flexibly encode a variety of cognitive spaces to meet the dynamic task demands.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the findings and previous literature.

claim: The left dlPFC was related to the expectancy-related attentional set upregulation.
source: Previous studies showed that the left dlPFC was related to the expectancy-related attentional set upregulation, while the right dlPFC was related to the online adjustment of control (Friehs et al., 2020; Vanderhasselt et al., 2009), which is consistent with our findings.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The right dlPFC was related to the online adjustment of control.
source: Previous studies showed that the left dlPFC was related to the expectancy-related attentional set upregulation, while the right dlPFC was related to the online adjustment of control (Friehs et al., 2020; Vanderhasselt et al., 2009), which is consistent with our findings.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The right PFC represents a composition of single rules.
source: Moreover, the right PFC also represents a composition of single rules (Reverberi et al., 2012), which may explain how the spatial Stroop and Simon types can be jointly encoded in a single space.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Reverberi et al., 2012.

claim: The brain can evaluate the cost and benefit associated with executing control for a demanding task according to the EVC theory.
source: Previous researchers have proposed an 'expected value of control (EVC)' theory, which posits that the brain can evaluate the cost and benefit associated with executing control for a demanding task, such as the conflict task, and specify the optimal control strength (Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shenhav et al., 2013.

claim: More frequently switching goals when doing a Stroop task were achieved by adjusting smaller control intensity.
source: For instance, Grahek et al., 2022 found that more frequently switching goals when doing a Stroop task were achieved by adjusting smaller control intensity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grahek et al., 2022.

claim: Different conflict conditions could be efficiently represented in a cognitive space encoded by the right dlPFC.
source: We found that different conflict conditions could be efficiently represented in a cognitive space encoded by the right dlPFC, and participants with stronger cognitive space representation have also adjusted their conflict control to a greater extent based on the conflict similarity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Participants with stronger cognitive space representation adjusted their conflict control to a greater extent based on the conflict similarity.
source: We found that different conflict conditions could be efficiently represented in a cognitive space encoded by the right dlPFC, and participants with stronger cognitive space representation have also adjusted their conflict control to a greater extent based on the conflict similarity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the brain-behavioral correlation analysis, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The cognitive space organization of conflicts guides cognitive control to adjust behavior.
source: The finding suggests that the cognitive space organization of conflicts guides cognitive control to adjust behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the brain-behavioral correlation results.

claim: Participants may adopt different strategies to represent a task, with model-based strategies benefitting goal-related behaviors more than model-free strategies.
source: Previous studies have shown that participants may adopt different strategies to represent a task, with the model-based strategies benefitting goal-related behaviors more than the model-free strategies (Rmus et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rmus et al., 2022.

claim: Cognitive space could serve as a mental model to assist fast learning and efficient organization of cognitive control settings.
source: Similarly, we propose that cognitive space could serve as a mental model to assist fast learning and efficient organization of cognitive control settings.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the findings.

claim: The cognitive space representation may provide a principle for how our brain evaluates the expected cost of switching and the benefit of generalization between states.
source: Specifically, the cognitive space representation may provide a principle for how our brain evaluates the expected cost of switching and the benefit of generalization between states and selects the path with the best cost–benefit tradeoff (Abrahamse et al., 2016; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The proximity between two states in cognitive space could reflect both the expected cognitive demand required to transition and the useful mechanisms to adapt from.
source: The proximity between two states in cognitive space could reflect both the expected cognitive demand required to transition and the useful mechanisms to adapt from.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the cognitive space framework.

claim: The closer two conditions are in cognitive space, the lower the expected switching cost and the higher the generalizability when transitioning between them.
source: The closer the two conditions are in cognitive space, the lower the expected switching cost and the higher the generalizability when transitioning between them.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the cognitive space framework.

claim: With the organization of a cognitive space, a new conflict can be quickly assigned a location in the cognitive space.
source: With the organization of a cognitive space, a new conflict can be quickly assigned a location in the cognitive space, which will facilitate the development of cognitive control settings for this conflict by interpolating nearby conflicts and/or projecting the location to axes representing different cognitive control processes, thus leading to a stronger CSE when following a more similar conflict condition.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of how cognitive space facilitates learning.

claim: Without a cognitive space, there would be no measure of similarity between conflicts on different trials, limiting the ability of fast learning of cognitive control setting from similar trials.
source: On the other hand, without a cognitive space, there would be no measure of similarity between conflicts on different trials, hence limiting the ability of fast learning of cognitive control setting from similar trials.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation contrasting with the cognitive space framework.

claim: The cognitive space in the right dlPFC appears to be an abstraction of concrete information from the visual regions.
source: The cognitive space in the right dlPFC appears to be an abstraction of concrete information from the visual regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the representational connectivity results.

claim: The right V1 and V2 encoded the spatial orientation of the target location.
source: We found that the right V1 and V2 encoded the spatial orientation of the target location (Figure 7) and showed strong representational connectivity with the right dlPFC (Figure 8), suggesting that there might be information exchange between these regions.
evidence: This is a result from the RSA and representational connectivity analyses, supported by Figures 7 and 8.

claim: There might be information exchange between right V1/V2 and right dlPFC.
source: We found that the right V1 and V2 encoded the spatial orientation of the target location (Figure 7) and showed strong representational connectivity with the right dlPFC (Figure 8), suggesting that there might be information exchange between these regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the representational connectivity results.

claim: The representation of spatial orientation may have provided the essential perceptual information to determine the conflict type.
source: We speculate that the representation of spatial orientation may have provided the essential perceptual information to determine the conflict type (Figure 1) and thus served as the critical input for the cognitive space.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: The conflict-type representation incorporates the stimulus–response mapping rules to the spatial orientation representation.
source: The conflict-type representation further incorporates the stimulus–response mapping rules to the spatial orientation representation, so that vertically symmetric orientations can be recognized as the same conflict type (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of how conflict type is represented, supported by Figure 4.

claim: The representation of conflict type involves the compression of perceptual information.
source: In other words, the representation of conflict type involves the compression of perceptual information (Flesch et al., 2022), which is consistent with the idea of a low-dimensional representation of cognitive control (Badre et al., 2021; MacDowell et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The compression and abstraction processes might be why the frontoparietal regions are the top of hierarchy of information processing.
source: The compression and abstraction processes might be why the frontoparietal regions are the top of hierarchy of information processing (Gilbert and Li, 2013) and why the frontoparietal regions are widely engaged in multiple task demands (Duncan, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The cognitive space did not depend on strategies that could be learned through training.
source: We found the conflict similarity modulation on CSE did not change with more training, indicating that the cognitive space did not depend on strategies that could be learned through training.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the training analysis results.

claim: The cognitive space should be determined by the intrinsic similarity structure of the task design.
source: Instead, the cognitive space should be determined by the intrinsic similarity structure of the task design.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the training analysis results.

claim: The CSE across different versions of spatial Stroop and flanker tasks was stronger than that across either of the two conflicts and Simon.
source: For example, a previous study (Freitas and Clark, 2015) has found that the CSE across different versions of spatial Stroop and flanker tasks was stronger than that across either of the two conflicts and Simon.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Freitas and Clark, 2015.

claim: The cognitive space generally exists to represent structured latent states, mental strategy cost, and social hierarchies.
source: Furthermore, recent studies showed that the cognitive space generally exists to represent structured latent states (e.g., Vaidya and Badre, 2022), mental strategy cost (Grahek et al., 2022), and social hierarchies (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cognitive space is likely a universal strategy that can be applied to different scenarios.
source: Therefore, cognitive space is likely a universal strategy that can be applied to different scenarios.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on previous research.

claim: The overall congruency effect was located at the medial frontal region (pre-SMA) in univariate analyses.
source: With conventional univariate analyses, we observed that the overall congruency effect was located at the medial frontal region (i.e., pre-SMA), which is consistent with previous studies (Botvinick et al., 2004; Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from the univariate fMRI analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Regions parametrically modulated by conflict-type difference showed right lateralization.
source: The right lateralization of these regions is consistent with a previous finding (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: The parametric encoding of conflict mirrors prior research showing the parametric encoding of task demands.
source: The parametric encoding of conflict also mirrors prior research showing the parametric encoding of task demands (Dagher et al., 1999; Ritz and Shenhav, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The scaling of brain activities based on conflict difference is potentially important to the representational organization of different types of conflicts.
source: The scaling of brain activities based on conflict difference is potentially important to the representational organization of different types of conflicts.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the univariate results.

claim: The conflict (dis)similarity is a combination of (dis)similarity of spatial Stroop and Simon conflicts.
source: One possible reason is that the conflict (dis)similarity is a combination of (dis)similarity of spatial Stroop and Simon conflicts, but each univariate region only reflects difference along a single conflict domain.
evidence: This is an explanation for why univariate regions did not show brain-behavioral relevance.

claim: The representational geometry is more of a multivariate problem than what univariate activities can capture.
source: Also likely, the representational geometry is more of a multivariate problem than what univariate activities can capture (Freund et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Freund et al., 2021b.

claim: Cognitive control can have its own form of representation that encompasses a dynamic process.
source: While it may not be as straightforward as the visual representation (e.g., creating a mental image from a real image in the visual area), cognitive control can have its own form of representation. An influential theory, Marr, 1982 three-level model proposed that representation serves as the algorithm of the process to achieve a goal based on the input. In other words, representation can encompass a dynamic process rather than being limited to static stimuli.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Marr, 1982.

claim: The representation of task profiles can be progressively constructed with time in the brain.
source: A similar idea has been proposed that the representation of task profiles can be progressively constructed with time in the brain (Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kikumoto and Mayr, 2020.

claim: The representation of cognitive space is most prominently involved at two critical stages to guide the transference of behavioral CSE.
source: Moreover, we anticipate that the representation of cognitive space is most prominently involved at two critical stages to guide the transference of behavioral CSE. The first stage involves the evaluation of control demands, where the representational distance/similarity between previous and current trials influences the adjustment of cognitive control. The second stage pertains to control execution, where the switch from one control state to another follows a path within the cognitive space.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about the temporal dynamics of cognitive space representation.

claim: The use of an experimental paradigm that permits parametric manipulation of conflict similarity provides a way to systematically investigate the organization of cognitive control.
source: The use of an experimental paradigm that permits parametric manipulation of conflict similarity provides a way to systematically investigate the organization of cognitive control, as well as its influence on adaptive behaviors.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The cross-subject RSA provides high sensitivity to the variables of interest and the ability to separate confounding factors.
source: Moreover, the cross-subject RSA provides high sensitivity to the variables of interest and the ability to separate confounding factors.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Cognitive control can both enhance the target representation and suppress the distractor representation.
source: We further showed cognitive control can both enhance the target representation and suppress the distractor representation (Figure 5E), which is in line with previous studies (Polk et al., 2008; Ritz and Shenhav, 2022).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis, supported by Figure 5E and citations.

claim: The behavioral CSE is not a pure measure of adjusted control but could be partly confounded by bottom-up factors such as feature integration.
source: However, since this paradigm is a two-alternative forced choice design, the behavioral CSE is not a pure measure of adjusted control but could be partly confounded by bottom-up factors such as feature integration (Hommel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: In the current design, the spatial Stroop and Simon effects are highly anticorrelated.
source: Another limitation is that in our design, the spatial Stroop and Simon effects are highly anticorrelated.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The study is not a comprehensive test of the cognitive space hypothesis but aimed primarily to provide original evidence for the geometry of cognitive space in representing conflict information.
source: Additionally, our study is not a comprehensive test of the cognitive space hypothesis but aimed primarily to provide original evidence for the geometry of cognitive space in representing conflict information in cognitive control.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The cognitive control can be parametrically encoded in the right dlPFC and guides cognitive control to adjust goal-directed behavior.
source: In sum, we showed that the cognitive control can be parametrically encoded in the right dlPFC and guides cognitive control to adjust goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the findings.

claim: Different cognitive control states may be encoded in an abstract cognitive space.
source: This finding suggests that different cognitive control states may be encoded in an abstract cognitive space, which reconciles the long-standing debate between the domain-general and domain-specific views of cognitive control and provides a parsimonious and more broadly applicable framework for understanding how our brains efficiently and flexibly represents multiple task settings.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the study.
